explanations.explanation: That's the plan in Heshbon. The people there say, "Come, let us cut her off from nationhood." It's a plot to wipe Moab off the map as a nation. I think that's a heavy plan to read about (Jeremiah 48:2).

Danger is what the plotters bring, not what they're cutting her off from. The plotters in Heshbon say, "Come, let us cut her off from nationhood." They want Moab to stop being a nation at all. Nobody in that plot is trying to take danger away (Jeremiah 48:2).

Sorrow is actually headed her way, friend. The plotters in Heshbon aren't trying to cut her off from it. What they say is, "Come, let us cut her off from nationhood." Their target is Moab's place among the nations (Jeremiah 48:2).

You got it, baker. On the ascent to Luhith, they weep bitterly as they go. This isn't a quiet walk with a few sniffles. I think this road is full of people whose hearts are breaking with every step (Jeremiah 48:5).
War songs aren't what the verse gives us, friend. The text says they weep bitterly as they go up to Luhith. The mood on that ascent is tears, and that's the picture the verse paints (Jeremiah 48:5).
Silence isn't what the verse describes, baker. The text says they weep bitterly as they go. Weeping is what fills that ascent (Jeremiah 48:5).
That's right. The cry on the way down to Horonaim says, "Flee! Run for your lives!" It's a cry to run, and run now. Not a cry to stroll (Jeremiah 48:5-6).

Close, but the text says otherwise. On the descent to Horonaim, the cries of distress say, "Flee! Run for your lives!" So the cry really does tell them to flee. It's a run-now kind of cry (Jeremiah 48:5-6).

Yes, baker. Chemosh goes into exile with his priests and officials. Chemosh is the god of the Moabites (1 Kings 11:33), and here he's the one going into exile. That's exactly what the verse says (Jeremiah 48:7).

That's not what the text says, friend. It says Chemosh will go into exile with his priests and officials. Rescuing someone is hard when you're the one packing your bags. Nobody gets saved by Chemosh here (Jeremiah 48:7).
No safekeeping in this verse, baker. The text says Chemosh will go into exile with his priests and officials. They're the ones leaving, not staying to keep anything safe (Jeremiah 48:7).
Not quite, friend. The LORD says the destroyer will move against every city, and "…not one town will escape." Every city is on the list, so there are no exceptions (Jeremiah 48:8).
Right on. The LORD says the destroyer will move against every city, and "…not one town will escape." Not a single one gets a pass. It's all of them, as the LORD has said (Jeremiah 48:8).

explanations.answer: Desolate with no one living in them
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The LORD says her cities will become desolate, with no one to dwell in them. Put salt on Moab, He says, for she will be laid waste. Empty streets where people used to live (Jeremiah 48:9).

explanations.answer: Crowded with people running from war
explanations.explanation: You'd think so with all that running, friend. But the LORD says her cities become desolate, with no one to dwell in them. Empty, not crowded. The streets go quiet (Jeremiah 48:9).

explanations.answer: Fortresses for the destroyer to keep
explanations.explanation: The destroyer doesn't move in, baker. The LORD says the cities will become desolate, with no one to dwell in them. Nobody is living there, destroyer included. Salt on Moab, and the places stand empty (Jeremiah 48:9).

explanations.answer: The one who holds back his sword from bloodshed
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The verse says, "…cursed is he who withholds his sword from bloodshed." It sits right beside the curse on the one who is remiss in doing the work of the LORD. It's a hard verse, and I think it's a heavy one to read (Jeremiah 48:10).

explanations.answer: The one who takes the treasures of Moab
explanations.explanation: Treasures don't show up in this curse, friend. The one named right alongside is the one who withholds his sword from bloodshed. Moab's treasures come up a few verses earlier, in verse 7. This curse is about the work of the LORD (Jeremiah 48:10).

explanations.answer: The one who mourns for the towns of Moab
explanations.explanation: Mourners aren't cursed here, baker. The verse says, "…cursed is he who withholds his sword from bloodshed." That's the second one. Mourning for Moab comes later, and it's something the neighbors are told to do (Jeremiah 48:10, 17).

Yes, baker. The text says, "…his flavor has remained the same, and his aroma is unchanged." Wine that never gets poured from vessel to vessel just sits there, settled on its dregs. The verse says Moab has not gone into exile (Jeremiah 48:11).
Sour isn't in the verse, friend. The LORD says, "…his flavor has remained the same, and his aroma is unchanged." The point is that it hasn't changed (Jeremiah 48:11).

That sounds nice, baker, but no. The LORD says, "…his flavor has remained the same, and his aroma is unchanged." Nothing got sweeter and nothing got worse. It's the same old flavor from the same old dregs (Jeremiah 48:11).

explanations.answer: Pour him out and shatter his jars
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The LORD says the wanderers "…will pour him out. They will empty his vessels and shatter his jars." The wine that sat still so long finally gets emptied. And the jars don't survive it (Jeremiah 48:12).

explanations.answer: Carry his jars off as plunder
explanations.explanation: That's not what these wanderers are said to do, baker. The text says they will pour him out, empty his vessels and shatter his jars. Pouring and shattering are the actions the verse names (Jeremiah 48:12).

explanations.answer: Tear down the walls around him
explanations.explanation: Walls aren't mentioned here, friend. The text says the wanderers will pour him out, empty his vessels and shatter his jars. The picture stays with the wine and the jars. Nothing about walls comes up in this verse (Jeremiah 48:12).
Yes, baker. The LORD says, "Then Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh…" Chemosh is the god of the Moabites (1 Kings 11:33). Back in verse 7, he's the one going into exile (Jeremiah 48:13, 48:7).
Baal isn't the name in this verse, friend. The LORD says, "Then Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh…" Chemosh is the god of the Moabites (1 Kings 11:33; Jeremiah 48:13).

Dagon was the god of the Philistines, baker (Judges 16:23). This verse names a different one. The LORD says, "Then Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh…" Chemosh was the god of the Moabites (1 Kings 11:33; Jeremiah 48:13).

I get why you'd think so, friend, but the text says the opposite. The King says the best of Moab's young men "…have gone down in the slaughter…" They don't win in this verse. They fall (Jeremiah 48:15).

That's right, baker. The King, whose name is the LORD of Hosts, says the best of Moab's young men "…have gone down in the slaughter…" There's no victory in that verse. It's a hard one to read (Jeremiah 48:15).

explanations.answer: It is at hand and rushing swiftly
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The verse says, "Moab’s calamity is at hand, and his affliction is rushing swiftly." No long wait on this one. It's already close and coming fast (Jeremiah 48:16).

explanations.answer: It will come after many generations
explanations.explanation: That's a lot of waiting, friend. But the verse says, "Moab’s calamity is at hand, and his affliction is rushing swiftly." It's close, not far off, so generations don't fit this one (Jeremiah 48:16).

explanations.answer: It will come at the end of the year
explanations.explanation: Nice try with the calendar, baker. The text gives no date, though. It says, "Moab’s calamity is at hand, and his affliction is rushing swiftly." That means close and fast, not a scheduled year-end (Jeremiah 48:16).
Not here, friend. The LORD says, "Mourn for him…" to everyone who surrounds him. Nobody is told to throw a party. Mourning is the instruction (Jeremiah 48:17).
Yes, baker. The LORD tells all who surround Moab, "Mourn for him…" and to tell how the mighty scepter is shattered. No celebrating is called for. It's a call to grieve (Jeremiah 48:17).

explanations.answer: The destroyer of Moab has come against her
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, baker. She's told to come down from her glory because "…the destroyer of Moab has come against you; he has destroyed your fortresses." Dibon is under attack. She's told to sit on parched ground (Jeremiah 48:18).

explanations.answer: She has turned away from the LORD her God
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say that, friend. The reason it gives is that "…the destroyer of Moab has come against you; he has destroyed your fortresses." I'd be careful not to add a reason the text doesn't give. It points to the destroyer (Jeremiah 48:18).

explanations.answer: Her king has been taken away as a captive
explanations.explanation: No king is mentioned in this verse, baker. The reason given is that "…the destroyer of Moab has come against you; he has destroyed your fortresses." The focus is on the destroyer and her fortresses. A captive king isn't in the text (Jeremiah 48:18).
Yes, friend, that's the word. The verse says, "Moab is put to shame, for it has been shattered." Shattered, like the jars in verse 12. The picture holds together (Jeremiah 48:20, 48:12).

Spared would be good news, baker, but the text doesn't say it. The verse says, "Moab is put to shame, for it has been shattered." Back in verse 8, the LORD says not one town will escape (Jeremiah 48:20, 48:8).
I wish it said healed, friend. But the verse says, "Moab is put to shame, for it has been shattered." Shattered is the word the LORD uses. Healing isn't mentioned in this passage (Jeremiah 48:20).

Yes, baker. The LORD closes with, "The horn of Moab has been cut off, and his arm is broken…" Both pictures are about Moab's strength being gone. Then the verse ends with, "…declares the LORD…" (Jeremiah 48:25).

It does say that, friend. The very last lines are, "The horn of Moab has been cut off, and his arm is broken…" declares the LORD. So the broken arm is right there at the close. I think it's a strong way to finish (Jeremiah 48:25).
